transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-02-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Lucas Chen (Redwood SE), Rajiv Menon (CTO, Apollo AI), Elena Cruz (ML Platform Lead), Tom Blake (Infra), Dr. Wei Zhou (Research)

Auto-summary: quick recap at the top, we discussed quantization strategy and runtime config for on-prem inference, agreed to run benchmark comparisons and a short pilot.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm maya, ae on the redwood team and lucas is our se. can you all do quick intros?
[00:12] Rajiv: yeah sure, rajiv here, cto at apollo. we're evaluating running our customer-facing models on-prem, mostly due to data residency and latency.
[00:20] Elena: elena, ml platform lead. primary concerns: throughput for batch jobs and tail latency for interactive stuff; also accuracy from quantization - we can't tolerate >2% perplexity regressions on our core model.
[00:34] Tom: tom, infra. running kubernetes on metal, we use a mix of a100s and older t4 fleet. sizing is tight right now.
[00:44] Lucas: great, thanks. so agenda: LT quantization tradeoffs (int8/fp8/gptq/awq), then runtime - kv cache, batching, kernel choices, then deployment model (private/vpc), then next steps.

[00:58] Maya: quick high-level -- AWQ has been promising on throughput + smaller memory but there are accuracy caveats depending on model and prompt distribution, gptq often gives better accuracy for some models but can be slower at inference time for some runtimes, and int8/FP8 are more native but require HW support.
[01:18] Dr. Wei: when you say slower for gptq, is that compile-time or per-token? we've seen variable results.
[01:25] Lucas: mostly per-token throughput because of additional dequant ops and less fused kernels; it depends on whether the runtime can fuse dequant + matmul into a single kernel. our runtime chooses kernels based on model architecture and sequence length distribution. if profiling shows dequant hotspots we prefer AWQ or tuned int8 kernels.

[01:48] Rajiv: our biggest concern is accuracy regression. We have customer SLAs that require median quality to be within 1.5% of FP16. How do you benchmark that?
[01:58] Maya: we recommend a 2-phase benchmark: 1) offline eval on your prompt sets to measure quality (perplexity, exact-match where applicable) comparing FP16, GPTQ, AWQ, INT8/FP8; 2) runtime end-to-end latency/throughput with your traces, including tail-latency p95/p99. we'll share our benchmark spreadsheet template.

[02:20] Elena: is awq deterministic? we need reproducible evals, otherwise it's hard to attribute regressions.
[02:26] Lucas: AWQ determinism is model-dependent; quantization randomness is usually from calibration and order of ops. we lock random seeds and use identical calibration datasets. also we capture output deltas and perform round-trip tests.

[02:44] Tom: about hardware: we have mixed gpus - some nodes are older. what's recommended? we can't rip and replace yet.
[02:50] Maya: for mixed fleets, our smart routing can send requests to compatible model variants; e.g., heavier fp16/gptq on a100 nodes, awq/int8 on cheaper hardware. That preserves latency SLO while reducing unit cost.

[03:10] Rajiv: latency targets: interactive endpoints need <150ms median and <300ms p95 with 8k context. can you hit that with awq/gptq?
[03:20] Lucas: probably yes with KV cache and batching tuned, but p95 is tricky for long contexts. KV cache reduces repeated context compute for chat-style calls; if you have many new prefixes then batching and kernel selection become more critical. for 8k sequences we recommend 1) prefix caching for common prefixes, 2) smaller batch windows for tail latency, 3) use kernel autotuning for large sequence lengths.

[03:50] Elena: quick clarification, we use a persistent kv-cache in our architecture; does redwood support optional on-disk or remote kv stores?
[03:58] Maya: our runtime supports memory-backed KV cache and can persist to local NVMe for warm-starts. remote kv stores are possible but add network latency, we typically keep cache local to the serving node and use smart routing to the node that holds the cache.

[04:20] Dr. Wei: what's the expected accuracy loss for AWQ vs GPTQ on a 7B model? any ballpark?
[04:27] Lucas: ballpark: GPTQ often stays within ~0.5-1% perplexity of FP16 if done carefully; AWQ can be competitive but in some prompt distributions we saw 1-3% delta. it depends a lot on activation distributions and calibration data. we always recommend running your eval set.

[04:48] Rajiv: can you share a typical benchmark we can run? we'd want to run on our infra.
[04:54] Maya: yes, we'll send the AWQ vs GPTQ spreadsheet, plus a docker image and a small harness to run end-to-end latency and perf counters. lucas will include recommended runtime flags.

[05:06] Tom: about batching, what's the tradeoff window? we can't increase latency too much.
[05:12] Lucas: there's a classic latency vs throughput curve. small batch windows (5-10ms) preserve low median latency but reduce throughput; larger windows (20-50ms) push throughput but increase median. our continuous batching packs requests into micro-batches; with prefix caching we can serve many chat calls with sub-150ms medians while still batching for token throughput.

[05:40] Elena: service reliability: for private deployment, what about SSO, audit logs, and kms?
[05:45] Maya: we support SAML SSO, audit logs, integration with customer KMS/HSM for model and request encryption keys, and per-tenant RBAC. we can provide SOC2 documentation.

[06:00] Rajiv: one of our customers requires isolation and we're thinking of VPC on-prem. how does redwood private handle network segmentation?
[06:07] Lucas: private offers a customer-controlled control plane with optional air-gapped on-prem package; network segmentation follows your internal VPC rules, and we can route inference traffic through private gateways. for strict isolation we recommend dedicated GPU pools per tenant.

[06:30] Dr. Wei: about kernel selection - you mentioned kernels for fused dequant+matmul. are those open-source or redwood-proprietary?
[06:38] Lucas: some kernels are upstream and we contribute; some of the optimized fused kernels are tuned in-house. we'll share ABI and tuning knobs. you can use our runtime open-source parts plus proprietary optimized kernels under license for Dedicated/Private customers.

[06:58] Rajiv: what's the onboarding time for private deployment on our k8s metal?
[07:04] Maya: pilot can start within 2-3 weeks after contract; full production depends on integration depth but typically 6-8 weeks for initial rollout. for air-gapped on-prem it needs more time for security review and packaging.

[07:20] Elena: any gotchas with mixed precision and fp8? I know fp8 is gaining traction but hardware support is early.
[07:28] Lucas: fp8 promises higher memory reduction vs int8 but requires hardware support (some newer accelerators have fp8 kernels). on a100/hippy there's partial support; our runtime can emulate fp8 with mixed precision but at a cost in latency. we typically use fp8 where hardware supports it natively.

[07:52] Tom: our fleet has mostly a100 and a few t4s; would you recommend homogenizing or using mixed routing?
[07:58] Maya: mixed routing is fine; Redwood's smart routing and model variants let you place lighter quantized models on cheaper nodes and fall back to higher-fidelity models on a100s for critical traffic.

[08:16] Rajiv: are there automated regression detectors when you rollout a new quantized model? we need guardrails.
[08:23] Lucas: yes, Redwood Optimize can run shadow evaluations on live traffic, compare output deltas, and trigger rollbacks if quality drifts beyond thresholds. you can set per-route thresholds.

[08:38] Dr. Wei: for calibration datasets, what size do you recommend?
[08:42] Lucas: for GPTQ/GPTQ-like calibrations usually 1-2k representative samples can be enough; AWQ calibration may need more diverse coverage, so we recommend 5-10k if you have varied prompts. the key is representativeness more than absolute size.

[09:00] Elena: any differences in memory footprint for awq vs gptq?
[09:05] Lucas: AWQ tends to have smaller memory footprint on disk and runtime thanks to optimized compressed layouts; GPTQ can be larger but depends on implementation. on-device KV cache size matters more for large contexts.

[09:22] Rajiv: so next steps - send benchmark artifacts and we'll run evals. timeline for pilot? ideally within 2 weeks.

[09:29] Maya: we'll aim to share artifacts today/tomorrow and schedule pilot kickoff; lucas and i will be primary contacts.

[09:40] -- mid-call deep dive into sample logs and kernel traces --
[09:45] Lucas: i'm showing a kernel flame for a 8k seq on a100. see these spikes at token generation - those are dequant ops for gptq, fused in newer builds. if we switch to awq and use our quantized matmul kernel it reduces dequant spikes but slightly increases some memory ops.
[10:10] Dr. Wei: can we get the kernel traces and perf counters?
[10:13] Lucas: yes i'll attach perf dumps and advise which perf counters to look at (memcpy, l2 hit rate, matmul throughput).

[10:30] Rajiv: on evaluation - aside from perplexity, we want semantic similarity and a small human eval for hallucination rates.
[10:36] Maya: agreed; we'll add semantic metrics and if you can share human eval labels we can help automate regression checks.

[10:50] Elena: any documented cases where AWQ failed badly for a model family?
[10:55] Lucas: in some adapter-heavy LLMs with many layernorm variants AWQ calibration needed per-layer tuning; without tuning you can see higher regressions. we document these and we can run model-specific tuning during the pilot.

[11:12] Tom: ops questions: for private deployment, how are upgrades handled? we need controlled rollouts.
[11:18] Maya: we support canary rollouts, A/B testing, automatic fallback to previous model versions, and cluster-level upgrade windows. you can set policies for automatic rollback on error rates or quality regressions.

[11:35] Rajiv: cost - ballpark for Dedicated/reserved vs hosted? we need a number to justify procurement.
[11:42] Maya: we'll share pricing ranges in the follow-up; generally dedicated reserved capacity reduces per-token cost but has a commit. private license varies with support level. i'll include a model for cost comparison in the spreadsheet.

[12:00] Elena: about telemetry retention and privacy - can we configure retention windows?
[12:06] Lucas: yes, telemetry retention is configurable; for sensitive workloads we support minimal retention or redaction and can route logs to customer-managed object storage.

[12:20] Rajiv: let's talk about success criteria for the pilot: 1) accuracy within 1.5% perplexity of FP16 on our eval set, 2) p95 latency <300ms for interactive, 3) cost reduction target of 30% vs current fp16 baseline.

[12:34] Maya: solid. we'll codify success criteria in the pilot doc.

[12:45] -- wrap-up --
[12:47] Maya: recap: we'll send the benchmark spreadsheet, docker harness, kernel traces, and price ranges. customer to share eval prompts and traces. lucas will prep runtime config. pilot kickoff to be scheduled next week.

[12:59] Rajiv: thanks all, looking forward.
[13:02] Elena: thanks.
